content.title: Here’s How to Watch Peacock Online for Free
content.text: Beginning as a DVD-by-mail rental service (how quaint) in the late 1990s, in 2007 Netflix delivered its billionth disc in the post, and also launched a video-on-demand service over the internet. With almost no competition, the company grew incredibly quickly, first acquiring big shows such as Breaking Bad in 2010, and then, the following year, making its very own, beginning with House of Cards. Still the market-leader today, Netflix may not have the biggest library of the streamers, but it arguably still leads the way in original programming – such as Bridgerton (with a new season out now), Stranger Things and Squid Game.How did we make our selection?In picking the very best Netflix has to offer, we’ve scoured through their menus, consulted The Telegraph’s own back-catalogue of reviews, and, of course, argued a lot within our team of TV journalists. Rest assured, every selection here has been agonised over and thoroughly appraised before making our list – which is growing all the time. If another great new programme drops, we’ll make sure we have it. We’re much better than an algorithm.Must-see show of the monthThis is a Gardening ShowLet’s be clear: Gardeners’ World this is not. The Hangover’s breakout star Zach Galifianakis has long since proven himself a master of simple deadpan comedy, unashamedly asking celebrities the exact questions they want to avoid in Between Two Ferns. Here he is in much more wholesome territory, with this offbeat six-part series that takes a very different approach to growing plants.Our review: The first thing to be said about This is a Gardening Show is that it’s not a gardening show, not by the British definition, anyway. Zach Galifianakis’s six-part horticultural tour is all about what we here would call kitchen gardening, but it is a little gem (lettuce pun intended).Skip to:Best drama shows on NetflixAdolescenceReuniting with director Philip Barantini of Boiling Point, and written by Jack Thorne, Stephen Graham’s drama came trailing expectation. And boy did it deliver – filmed in one-take, as with Boiling Point, it tells the story of a 13-year-old child who is accused of murdering a classmate. Splicing together topical concerns over the manosphere and Andrew Tate, as well as perennial parental worries, it’s an utterly terrifying, and utterly compelling, watch.Our review: If you’re a parent to a school-age boy, I don’t know whether I should advise you to watch Adolescence (Netflix) immediately, or avoid it at all costs because it will chill your blood.American PrimevalThere is a popular idea of the American Wild West as an era of myth and romance, opportunity and adventure. In this dark six-part Western, however, the untamed no man’s land of 19th-century Utah is an apocalyptic crucible of cruelty and death; a lawless wilderness fought over by the United States Army, the Mormon militia, Native Americans and pioneers. “Doesn’t seem to be a world that favours a woman on her own,” says settler Sara (Betty Gilpin), a mother with a bounty on her head. And yet, for Sara and her son Devin (Preston Mota), there is no choice but to make it to the other side, guided begrudgingly by a lonely frontiersman called Isaac (Taylor Kitsch). The series is written by Mark L Smith, who co-wrote the similarly bleak 2015 film The Revenant.Our review: American Primeval portrays the Old West as such a hellhole that it makes Taylor Sheridan’s rugged Westerns (Yellowstone, 1883) look like an episode of Escape to the Country.Baby ReindeerControversy over the stated claim that this is “a true story” engulfed Baby Reindeer, but why not watch it and judge it for yourself? Originally a one-man theatre show, which Scottish comedian Richard Gadd wrote about his experience of having a stalker, it’s now a chilling drama starring Gadd as a version of himself and the terrific Jessica Gunning as Martha – a woman he befriends, and who proceeds to bombard him with increasingly alarming messages. But to what extent does Donny encourage her, and how does it link to trauma from his past? This expertly paced series keeps you guessing.Our review: Like Patrick Melrose in Edward St Aubyn’s remarkable series of novels, there is something thrilling in watching a man self-combust.BeefRage. That’s the emotion coursing through this blistering dark parable, which kicks off with a road rage incident involving two on-edge Asian-American drivers who then become consumed by revenge. Lifestyle entrepreneur Amy is close to finally selling her small business, but is constantly patronised by her white buyer and has a smugly chilled-out husband at home – no wonder she keeps fondling her secretly stashed gun. Struggling builder Danny is under pressure to support his whole family, and has a volatile ex-con cousin. There’s a gleeful catharsis in their explosive feud that the viewer may well share.Our review: The afters are the main course in Beef , a windmilling revenge drama for the 21st century that begins in the unlikely confines of a hardware store car park.Breaking Bad/Better Call SaulIf you missed out on one of the great dramas of our time and its equally powerful spin-off series, or if you just want to revisit them both, here’s your chance. Vince Gilligan’s landmark crime series Breaking Bad sees feeble chemistry teacher Walter White transform into a brutal meth-making kingpin after he receives a cancer diagnosis. Bryan Cranston is extraordinary as a man gaining power but losing his soul. The sterling cast also features Aaron Paul, Anna Gunn, Dean Norris, Jonathan Banks and Betsy Brandt, while Bob Odenkirk as criminal lawyer Saul proved such a fan-favourite that he got his own show.Our Better Call Saul review: Amid the tension, rollicking dialogue and flashes of violence, Better Call Saul’s winning attribute continues to be its slow-burn consistency.Black DovesA top-flight cast and a glittering Christmas-time London backdrop help keep eyes adhered to this upbeat six-episode caper starring Keira Knightley as Helen Webb, a highly trained operative for a commercial spy agency who also just happens to be the British Defence Secretary’s (Andrew Buchan) wife and the mother of their two children. Add a plot predicated on the mysterious murder of her government-advisor lover and a nebulous international conspiracy involving a recently deceased Chinese ambassador, plus Sarah Lancashire as Webb’s hard-as-nails handler and Ben Whishaw as her freelance-assassin best friend, and you begin to appreciate just how far from reality we are going to get.Our review: If your idea of a good time is a slightly grubby Whishaw dragging you into a series of escalating gunfights, then Christmas has come early.Black MirrorCharlie Brooker moved his dystopian sci-fi series from Channel 4 to Netflix, gaining a bigger budget while retaining its chilling mission statement: exploring the nightmarish possible endpoint of modern technology. Brooker also used his new home to boldly experiment with form, creating an interactive film, Bandersnatch, in which the decisions you make as a viewer dictate the storyline (like the Choose Your Own Adventure books). But the standard episodes are inventive too, each riffing on a different genre and penetrating idea, and boast big-name guest stars like Bryce Dallas Howard, Jesse Plemons, Andrea Riseborough, Maxine Peake and Andrew Scott.Black RabbitJude Law and Jason Bateman star in a restaurant-based crime thriller; even gloomier than The Bear, if you can believe such a thing is possible. The duo play siblings and former bandmates, but while Law’s Jake is now running a successful New York nightspot, Bateman’s Vince is a chaotic addict, running from the mob, who Jake unwisely brings back into the fold.Our review: If you’re looking for a more sophisticated alternative to the current glut of unhinged dramas – The Girlfriend, The Guest, Coldwater, all of which feature bonkers behaviour – then try Black Rabbit.BridgertonDearest gentle reader, the period drama is back with a bang – quite literally. Shonda Rhimes’s mega-hit adaptation of Julia Quinn’s romance novels gives viewers Regency-era fashions, balls and heaving bosoms, but cannily updates the genre with diverse casting, feminist(ish) sensibilities and properly steamy sex scenes. Nicola Coughlan is the breakout star as the wallflower who wields power through her gossip-columnist alter ego. With each season focussing on the courtship of a different sibling in the massive titular family, following the eight books in Quinn’s series, Bridgerton should keep providing its frothy escapist pleasures for some time to come.Our review: A sparkling regency romance, Bridgerton is the sort of series that slips down as easily as a glass of pre-dinner champagne.Cobra KaiStarting off as a YouTube spin-off to the 1984 teen classic Karate Kid, this series has thrived since its transfer to Netflix. The final five-episode mini-series concludes its trajectory in fine style – modulating cheese, nostalgia and heartfelt sweetness.Our review: If only all nostalgia trips were as rewarding as Cobra Kai. The 1980s is an ongoing obsession for the entertainment industry. No series handles that better than Cobra Kai, which understands that, though the past has its charms, it’s the stories told today that matter most.The CrownAdmittedly Peter Morgan’s royal saga started more strongly than it finished, but it remains a sumptuously detailed, sharply written and frequently riveting drama. It also features one of the all-time-great ensemble casts, cleverly refreshed every couple of seasons – from established talent such as Olivia Colman, Imelda Staunton, Jonathan Pryce, Alex Jennings, Gillian Anderson and Lesley Manville to star-making turns from the likes of Claire Foy, Vanessa Kirby, Erin Doherty, Josh O’Connor and Emma Corrin. Together, they create an empathetic snapshot of the royal family during a pivotal period of change in our nation’s history.Our review: Drama doesn’t come more eagerly awaited than The Crown. This 10-part production, which chronicles the lives of the Windsors from 1947 to 1956, is rumoured to have cost £100 million, which would make it the most expensive TV series in history.Death by Lightning, NetflixA Netflix series that doesn’t overstay its welcome at only four parts, this pacy and at times very funny, drama tells the compelling story of US President James Garfield (Michael Shannon) and Charles Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen, never better) the delusional, seemingly bumbling loner who would go on to kill Garfield.Our review: James Garfield was President of the United States for 200 days. In British terms, that’s about four-and-a-half Liz Trusses.Dept QVery much Netflix’s answer to Amazon’s Slow Horses, with a recalcitrant lead (Matthew Goode) being dumped into a dead-end cold case department in the Edinburgh police force. Although based on the novels by the Danish author Jussi Adler-Olsen, the location has, obviously, been switched by screenwriter Scott Frank (The Queen’s Gambit). Goode clearly relishes playing against his usual clean-cut type as detective Carl Morck, with able support from Mark Bonnar and Kelly Macdonald, plus a slate of pitch-black crimes to investigate.Our review: If you’d been wondering what happened to Scandi noir, all brutal and gloomy, well, here it is – it just went away, popped into Slough House for some tips and was next seen alive and well in Scotland.EricBenedict Cumberbatch stars as Vincent Anderson, a genius puppeteer in 1980s New York whose nine-year-old son Edgar goes missing, in this new noir-ish drama. Granted we’ve seen countless lost child thrillers in the past few years, but this rich psychological work by acclaimed British writer Abi Morgan is a very different proposition. Not only does Vincent’s creation, a 7ft blue furry Muppets-type creature called Eric, become a sort of invisible friend to the despairing father, this ambitious tale also looks at everything from intergenerational conflict to a city in crisis. It’s unflinching, courageous, career-best work from Cumberbatch.Our review: At heart, this is a straightforward story – no flashbacks or complicated timelines – in which a detective investigates the child’s disappearance, and the child’s desperate parents cling on to hope as best they can.House of CardsThis sharp, cynical political drama, along with Orange Is the New Black, set the standard for Netflix’s original output. An American remake of the legendary 1990s BBC series, it saw Kevin Spacey succeed Ian Richardson as the Machiavellian, power-hungry operator Francis Urquhart, who lurks in the shadows and confides his cunning plans to the viewer in the style of a Shakespearean soliloquy. Spacey is deliciously evil, Robin Wright is fascinatingly slippery as his wife Claire, and the quality supporting cast features Michael Kelly, Patricia Clarkson, future Oscar-winner Mahershala Ali, and a pre-Marvelous Mrs Maisel Rachel Brosnahan.Our review: Can House of Cards’s fictional Oval Office megalomaniac still hold our attention, when there’s a real-life White House luridly lurching from crisis to crisis?LupinCentring on Omar Sy’s exceedingly suave Assane Diop, a master thief in the vein of his fictional hero Arsène Lupin, this French mystery series is supremely stylish entertainment. If, like me, you love a clever heist that involves elaborate disguises and Olympic-level cat burglar athleticism, Lupin delivers again and again – but there’s also some sincere long-term plotting around a terrible event in his childhood, his thirst for justice, and how his criminal activities impact on his family life. The super-cool Sy is both action hero and charismatic secret agent: basically James Bond, but very French.Our review: This is a Boys’ Own tale, which our dashing hero pulls off with huge charm, plenty of heart and a hefty dose of adrenaline.MaidRising star Margaret Qualley leads this moving drama based on Stephanie Land’s memoir. Qualley plays Alex Russell, who escapes her abusive boyfriend and tries to make a new life with two-year-old daughter Maddy while working as a maid. However, as she has no fixed address, she’s constantly thwarted by ridiculous red tape in a system that more often harms than helps. Andie MacDowell (Qualley’s actual mother) is wrenching too as Alex’s mum, who has a serious but undiagnosed mental health disorder. Throughout, Qualley’s connection with the wonderful Rylea Neveah Whittet as Maddy gives the series its heart and its fight.MindhunterNetflix has lured numerous auteurs from cinema, and their major get here is the director David Fincher. His fingerprints are all over this lethal psychological thriller, which takes place in the late 1970s as the FBI was just beginning to profile murderers and serial killers. Mindhunter, as with Fincher movies like Zodiac, features his taut plotting, recognisable green tint, nauseating sense of dread, and bravura long scenes that build heart-pounding drama simply through a conversation between two people. Jonathan Groff and Holt McCallany, as the FBI agents, and Anna Torv as their closeted lesbian psychotherapist colleague lead this criminally good show.Our review: Mindhunter is grown-up television that compels you to think about shifting attitudes in society.Money HeistThe definition of a sleeper hit, this Spanish-language Netflix original was initially intended as a two-part limited series. But the success of the first season – which follows a group of strangers recruited to stage robberies of the Royal Mint of Spain and the Royal Bank of Spain – lead to a further four seasons, which shadowed increasingly daring and globe-trotting exploits. It made an international star of Álvaro Morte and, like Lupin, brought an ineffable brand of Euro-cool to an otherwise tired genre. Just don’t mention the title, which reads like something churned out during a particularly lacklustre ChatGPT session.Our review: Bank robbers are not renowned for their subtlety, but even by the profession’s traditional standards the cast of Money Heist (Netflix) are an attention-seeking bunchNarcosThis, ahem, fiendishly addictive 1980s Colombia-set drama tells the story of drug lord Pablo Escobar and the DEA agents sent to hunt him down. Goodfellas is a clear influence here, both in form (voiceover features heavily) and in the gradual ratcheting up of corruption and sickening violence. Wagner Moura is horribly compelling as Escobar, portraying him as a contradictory man whose failed ambitions have fatal consequences for those around him, while Pedro Pascal (who has since become a Hollywood A-lister thanks to The Mandalorian and The Last of Us) is equally strong as one of the lawmen on his tail.Our review: Drugs, women, wealth and mass murder: the life of Colombian drug baron Pablo Escobar carries seismic dramatic potential. And yet we’ve rarely seen him played on the big – or small – screen. Until now.One DayLeo Woodall as Dexter and Ambika Mod as Emma - Ludovic Robert/NetflixBanish the woeful movie, and its weirdly miscast Anne Hathaway, from your mind. David Nicholls’s endearing 2009 novel – about two opposites-attract students who meet at the end of university, and then keep reconnecting on the same date, St Swithin’s Day, over 20 years – finally gets a worthy adaptation in the form of this romantic, occasionally painful, far more authentic series. Ambika Mod and Leo Woodall (who recently impressed, respectively, in This Is Going to Hurt and White Lotus) fit perfectly in those lead roles, and a cracking cast features Eleanor Tomlinson, Joely Richardson and Toby Stephens. Achingly nostalgic.Our review: It’s the most bingeable Netflix offering since Emily in Paris – deep as a puddle in a drought, but sometimes isn’t that exactly what you want?One Hundred Years of SolitudeNetflix brings Nobel Prize-winner Gabriel García Márquez’s exceptional, sweeping magical-realist novel to life. It expertly weaves together the story of seven generations of the Buendia family, whose patriarch, Jose Arcadio Buendía (Marco González), founded the fictional town of Macondo – and ruminates on how we cannot escape our past, or our fate. Claudio Cataño is brilliant as his revolutionary-son. Shot in García Márquez’s native Colombia in subtitled Spanish.Our review: Such is the reverence with which Gabriel García Márquez’s Nobel prize-winning novel One Hundred Years of Solitude is held that surely trying to turn its towering themes and magic-realist imagination into a TV series would have to be a fool’s game. How do you film the unfilmable?Orange Is the New BlackNetflix made a real statement of intent in the first year of its original programming with this bold comedy/drama. Based on Piper Kerman’s memoir, it follows an upper-middle-class white woman who is sent to a federal prison after her former girlfriend names her as a drug smuggler. It quickly expands into a layered, funny and sometimes devastating ensemble portrait, spotlighting characters like Uzo Aduba’s Crazy Eyes, Danielle Brooks’s Taystee, and Natasha Lyonne’s Nicky. There are serious critiques around race, class, addiction and more, but its most radical act is simply humanising these flawed but lovable inmates.Our review: When women’s prison drama Orange Is the New Black arrived on Netflix in 2013, it gave viewers something rarely seen on television: an ensemble of diverse and three-dimensional female characters.OzarkThose looking for a follow-up to Breaking Bad should head for “the Ozarks” (a lakeside region in Missouri), where financial advisor Marty Byrde flees with his family as part of a money laundering deal with a Mexican drug cartel in this atmospheric thriller. Jason Bateman and Laura Linney play the outwardly respectable couple juggling marriage and parenthood with turf warfare once the resident criminals figure out their scheme. It’s densely plotted, darkly funny, and features virtuoso performances from Julia Garner as a bright local girl doomed by her family and Janet McTeer as the cartel’s smooth-talking attorney.Our review: The appeal of the show is ultimately rooted in the Linney-Bateman double act. She is chilling as a wife and mother who has found her true calling later in life as heartless criminal. Bateman, for his part, rises reliably to the occasion as her oleaginous spouse.The Queen’s GambitAnya Taylor-Joy exploded into public consciousness via this unlikely hit: a miniseries revolving around a chess prodigy. Of course, it helps that her character Beth Harmon (who first appeared in Walter Tevis’s 1983 novel) is also a rebellious orphan with a destabilising drink and drugs habit, as well as a lone woman in a world of men. Add in covetable 1950s-60s costumes, Cold War tensions, ingenious dramatisation of chess games, and idiosyncratic love interests played by Harry Melling, Jacob Fortune-Lloyd and Thomas Brodie-Sangster, and you’ve got an unbeatable strategy.Red Riding TrilogyFirst shown on Channel 4 in 2009, this gritty adaptation of David Peace’s Yorkshire-set series of novels was a quiet hit, and featured an excellent young cast that all went on to big things. Set around the investigation into the Yorkshire Ripper, the story delves into police corruption and organised crime.Our review: It is arguably the best British ensemble cast ever put together for television, and in the actors attracted to the scripts and Peace’s source material, Red Riding showed that TV was just as worthy of any A-Lister’s attention as movies.RipleyAudiences can’t get enough of Patricia Highsmith’s psychopathic conman Tom Ripley. Now we can add to the list of previous excellent adaptations Steven Zaillian’s moody, spellbinding noir series. It stars Andrew Scott as a cold-blooded predator who gradually infiltrates the charmed Amalfi Coast life of wastrel rich kid Dickie Greenleaf, played by Johnny Flynn. Robert Elswit’s astonishing, expressionistic monochrome cinematography – both beautiful and unsettling – recalls Cold War classics like The Third Man, ramping up the tension and paranoia. Maurizio Lombardi’s inspector is a great addition in later episodes, as is a scene-stealing Maine Coon cat.SirensThe lives of the super-rich, delineated in all its nauseating glory, is a current TV staple, and while not quite up there with the likes of Succession and The White Lotus, this five-part series created by Molly Smith Metzler and based on her 2011 play Elemeno Pea, is still a superior satire. It follows down-at-heel Devon DeWitt (The White Lotus’s Meghann Fahy) visiting her estranged sister, Simone (Milly Alcock), who is working as a personal assistant for a super-rich couple (superbly played by Julianne Moore and Kevin Bacon). What she encounters is a weirdly rarefied world where favourite chocolate is “overnighted from Japan” and the in-house chef serves up ever more elaborate smoothies. Devon’s instinct? To extricate her sibling from this insane world.Our review: The main pleasure is in the ridiculous details of the Kells’ lifestyle, from bird funerals and perfumed underwear to Michaela asking her PA to script sexy matrimonial text messages.Squid GameWho could have predicted that a dystopian Korean series about economic disparity, featuring players taking part in deadly versions of children’s games to win life-changing prize money, all for the amusement of an elite cabal, would become Netflix’s most-watched programme? Yet that’s what happened in September 2021, as more than 142 million households in 94 countries clocked up 1.65 billion viewing hours by tuning into Hwang Dong-hyuk’s utterly gripping Squid Game. It’s even inspired a similarly binge-worthy spin-off competition, Squid Game: The Challenge, in which real people don the iconic green tracksuits (no actual deaths involved, though).Our review: Amid the bloodshed and gunsmoke, it is often forgotten that the original Squid Game had a tongue-in-cheek energy that, at times, veered towards a sort of violent camp.Stranger ThingsThe small town of Hawkins, Indiana, looks like suburban paradise – but there are secrets lurking just beyond the white picket fences. The Duffer Brothers’ 1980s-set sci-fi series pays homage to the greats of the genre (Stephen King, John Carpenter, David Lynch, Steven Spielberg) in its compelling combination of coming-of-age drama and jump-scare supernatural horror. Millie Bobby Brown is the standout as Eleven, a girl with telepathic abilities who was experimented on by evil scientists, but each character, from the kids to the grown-ups, is written with loving detail – including Winona Ryder’s single mother and David Harbour’s gruff police chief.Our review of the final episode: The appeal of Stranger Things has always been rooted in nostalgia for the 1980s, and so it is fitting that the last-ever episode of the Netflix blockbuster should hark back to a lost era of big weepy television send-offs.Top BoyThe first two seasons of Ronan Bennett’s award-winning drama aired on Channel 4, and, following a campaign led by Canadian rapper Drake, Netflix then commissioned seasons three to five. Set on a Hackney estate, it’s a devastating portrait of gang violence, drug dealing and sheer desperation: no one in Top Boy has any better options. In that sense it’s reminiscent of David Simon’s The Wire, and Bennett similarly builds out his world with fully-formed, all-too-believable characters. Ashley Walters is particularly strong as Dushane, but excellent too are Kane Robinson, Araloyin Oshunremi, Jasmine Jobson, Saffron Hocking, and Micheal Ward.Our review: Six years might have passed but things aren’t getting any easier on the Hackney mean streets where the more things change the more they stay depressingly the same.Toxic TownNo one would have expected Netflix viewers the world over to want to watch a drama featuring the inner workings of Corby Borough Council, but Jack Thorne’s four-part series is a compelling take on a particularly British real-life scandal. Jodie Whittaker plays Susan McIntyre, whose son is poisoned by toxic waste run-off, and takes up the fight against the culprits, British Steel. A sprightly David and Goliath tale, even it might baffle international viewers.Our review: It is a real-life David and Goliath tale, and in the scrappy Susan McIntyre, one of the mothers whose child was affected, they have an Erin Brockovich figure.Yellowstone CollectionTaylor Sheridan has spun a vast and rugged world in his Yellowstone series, which includes multiple spin-offs that span from 1883 to the present day. In the first series, Kevin Costner stars as the patriarch of the Dutton family, owners of the largest cattle ranch in Montana, as land developers attempt to invade his territory. Prequels 1883 (starring Sam Elliott and Faith Hill) and 1923 (starring Harrison Ford and Helen Mirren) have also proven popular. More series from the franchise are likely to be added in future.WednesdayTim Burton’s glorious Addams Family spin-off follows daughter Wednesday (Jenna Ortega in a star-making turn) as she enrols in Nevermore Academy and ends up solving a murder. Much like the films, it’s a gothic aesthetic vision of macabre humour and style. Luis Guzmán and Catherine Zeta Jones also star as Gomez and Morticia.Our review of season two: An addictively macabre second season that confirms the stardom of lead actress Jenna Ortega.Best comedy shows on NetflixHow to Get to Heaven from BelfastAnother scintillating comedy romp from the writer of Channel 4’s riotous smash hit Derry Girls, Lisa McGee. This eight-parter is set in contemporary Ireland and centres on a trio of older – but equally unhinged – friends in their late 30s, lured to the funeral of an old schoolfriend by a long-buried secret. It’s not long before they’re dragged into a hilariously chaotic chase across Ireland. The chemistry between the three leads, Sinéad Keenan, Caoilfhionn Dunne and Roisin Gallagher, is red hot and a galaxy of other familiar Irish faces – Ardal O’Hanlon, Bronagh Gallagher, Emmett J Scanlan, Michelle Fairley are superb in support.Our review: Producing a follow-up to Derry Girls was a tough ask, but writer Lisa McGee has delivered. This is a murder mystery infused with the comic brilliance of her earlier work.A Man on the InsideCheers’ Ted Danson stars in this terrific new eight-part comedy caper about a retired San Francisco professor who is hired to infiltrate a corrupt nursing home. It is written by The Good Place creator Michael Schur, who is a whizz at balancing sentimentality with laughs. Case in point: a delightful montage involving pensioners auditioning for the job of a spy. Sally Struthers, Mary Elizabeth Ellis and Marc Evan Jackson make up the rest of the strong ensemble cast.Our review: It is comedy without satirical barbs, but delivered with complete command, tempering a regular drumbeat of good gags and daft set-ups with some trenchant commentary on ageing and memory.Man vs BabyRowan Atkinson’s follow-up to Man vs Bee (2022) comes with the TV’s second-best farting moment of 2025 (The Celebrity Traitors being the first). Reprising his role as hapless Trevor Bingley, he’s coaxed out of retirement from his house-sitting career for one last job, looking after a tech-packed high-end London penthouse. As if that doesn’t already bode ill, he discovers it comes with a baby whom he has to look after. If anything, this exceeds the earlier production, introducing a welcome layer of sentiment and surprise alongside the perfectly-honed slapstick.Our review: It is unlikely that anyone was clamouring for a sequel to Man vs Bee… However, Atkinson and co-writer William Davies have retooled the premise and, in the process, have created the most unexpectedly lovely winter warmer.GLOWWho knew there was once a women’s wrestling circuit called GLOW (Gorgeous Ladies of Wrestling)? Liz Flahive and Carly Mensch’s vibrant series revisits this gonzo 1980s marvel: think big hair, spandex, headlocks, and unconventional girl power. Marc Maron is a hoot as the misanthropic director Sam, but the core of the show is the wrecked friendship between former soap star Debbie (Betty Gilpin) and desperately ambitious actress Ruth (Alison Brie) – which translates into a fiery rivalry in the ring. Naturally, Ruth’s heel character is a boo-hiss Soviet, while Debbie is the all-American beauty. Offbeat, vivid and weirdly charming.Our review: One of the best things about GLOW is the sheer Eighties-ness of it all – it’s a sensory explosion of synth-heavy tunes, neon lights, high-cut leotards, hairspray… and even a robot which dispenses cocaine.I Think You Should Leave with Tim RobinsonIt’s hard to imagine this surreal sketch series existing before the advent of streaming, or reaching the kind of wide audience that it has while on Netflix. But we’re all better off for having it in our lives. Co-creator (with Zach Kanin) Robinson, who also stars, is an absurdist genius who pushes cringe comedy to its limits. His obsessive characters, whether an ornery man in a focus group or a guy dressed as a hotdog, refuse to back down – and in the process all social niceties and structures come crashing down. It’s startlingly funny, and the end of every sketch zags in a different direction.Our review: It’s almost impossible to write about the genre-warping series without sounding like you’re trying to craft a high-minded PhD about the very nature of comedy.No Good DeedLiz Feldman follows her Emmy-winning yet oddly underrated dark comedy Dead to Me with another slice of mischief in a similar vein, a very smart conceit cleverly executed by a crack cast equally at home with drama and comedy. Lisa Kudrow and Ray Romano are at the heart of the enigmatic narrative as married couple Lydia and Paul, watching as an array of interested parties have a poke around the palatial LA villa which they have consented to put on the market after… Well, what precisely has prompted it is revealed in increments over eight episodes, but could well involve a past tragedy, debts owed to the wrong people and long-buried secrets both physical and emotional.Our review: No Good Deed is a strange amalgam of the silly, the sad and the quite funny that could only have come from the modern-day streaming economy.Sex EducationTalk about versatility. Gillian Anderson can give us both a frosty Margaret Thatcher in The Crown and the robustly candid therapist Jean Milburn in this carnally frank, but ultimately big-hearted, comedy. Asa Butterfield is brilliant too as her repressed teenage son Otis, who becomes an unofficial sex therapist himself for his confused classmates. This exceptionally well-cast show has been a star-making project for many – including ex-Doctor Who leading man Ncuti Gatwa and Simone Ashley, who went on to Bridgerton fame. Girls’s Jemima Kirke is excellent too as a seemingly cool headmistress with a hidden agenda.Our review: This addictive new comedy drama from Laurie Nunn which was written as a love letter to those American High School movies such as John Hughes’s The Breakfast Club.Unbreakable Kimmy SchmidtThe wacky premise of Tina Fey and Robert Carlock’s brilliant sitcom is that Kimmy has been held hostage in a doomsday bunker for 15 years – but now she’s free. Hilarious! Actually, it really is, thanks to a perfectly judged performance by Ellie Kemper and support from Tituss Burgess as her camp actor roommate, Carol Kane as her take-no-prisoners landlady, Jane Krakowski as her socialite employer, and a very creepy Jon Hamm as the reverend who abducted Kimmy. The lightning-fast episodes have a phenomenal joke rate, including some ridiculously good song parodies (Burgess’s Peeno Noir is unforgettable).Best documentaries on NetflixAttack on London: Hunting the 7/7 BombersIn a year that was, understandably, replete with programming about the 2005 attack, Netflix’s own effort immediately distinguished itself by starting with the voice of one of the suicide bombers. It’s an unsettling, attention-grabbing way to begin, but the four-parter then goes on to display a real maturity and thoroughness in how it unpacks the story, including a long-forgotten moment on breakfast TV in which Kate Garraway interviews a passenger fresh off the Tube, and, because they are Muslim, she asks them to condemn terrorism on behalf of Muslims everywhere. But it’s the interviews that live long in the memory, with survivors, first-responders and those who made the decisions about how Britain should react – including Tony Blair.Our review: There are unforgettable stories here from people whose lives were forever changed by the attack.Formula 1: Drive to SurviveOne of the best among Netflix’s riveting sports documentaries, Drive to Survive takes us behind the scenes of an F1 season, following ten teams and their drivers, from 2018 onwards. This surprise hit has brought a massive new international audience (including, crucially, American viewers) to the sport by focussing on the people: the juicy rivalries, the very different leadership styles, the clashing egos, and the peculiar challenge of your teammate becoming your adversary (see: Max Verstappen and Sergio Perez). All punctuated by deafening races and the occasional terrifying near-fatal crash. No wonder this series has roared to victory.Our review: Prepare yourself for fabulous aerial shots which reek of streaming cash, shiny mobile homes being panned across slowly and ostensibly behind-the-scenes footage, albeit only from the exact scenes the protagonists are happy for you to look behind.The Last DanceWhat does it take to reach the top – and stay there? This gripping 10-part documentary gives you a courtside seat to the astonishing ability and psyche of one such figure, basketball hero Michael Jordan, as he prepares for his final season (1997-98) with the Chicago Bulls. The level of access is unusually good, and director Jason Hehir alternates between absorbing archive footage and enlightening contemporary interviews with everyone from Bulls head coach Phil Jackson to Jordan teammates Dennis Rodman and Scottie Pippen and superfans such as Barack Obama. It is pretty hagiographic, but the Jordan legend is simply irresistible.Louis Theroux: Inside the ManosphereThe documentary-maker looks at the manosphere – an online collection of ultra-masculine influencers, exemplified by men such as Andrew Tate. Theroux meets some of the phenomenon’s big players – and discovers the worrying allure their lavish lifestyles and sexual freedoms hold for impressionable young men.Our review: Theroux’s encounters with a succession of cigar-smoking gym bros revving their Lamborghinis and overclocking their lives are riveting. Skewering the self-styled ubermensches is fish-in-a-barrel stuff for a seasoned operator such as Theroux.Making a MurdererThe urtext of the industry’s now-mammoth true crime obsession, Making a Murderer is a phenomenally dedicated piece of work by its directors Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos. They spent 10 years filming the first season, chronicling the arrest of Steven Avery in Manitowoc County, Wisconsin, his subsequent conviction for sexual assault and attempted murder, and then another, even more controversial case involving Avery and his nephew Brendan Dassey. It’s both a forensically detailed indictment of a monstrously flawed justice system and an absorbing real-life murder mystery, with more twists and turns than you could possibly script.Our review of Making a Murder Part 2: Series two has a broader sweep as it considers the institutional imbalances and disjointedness of American justice.Our Planet/Our Planet IIThe BBC’s long reign as nature documentary-makers supreme is under threat thanks to this jaw-dropping, multimillion-pound series by the team behind Planet Earth. They’ve even nabbed David Attenborough – the cheek! The result is two blockbuster spectacles anchored by Attenborough’s unparalleled commentary as we range from hunting dogs tracking a wildebeest calf in the Serengeti, to penguins feeding on Arctic krill and the courtship dance of the manakin. The series also goes much further than their BBC rivals in demonstrating the devastating effects of climate change on our natural world and why it’s imperative that we act now.Our review: Worn down by nearly a century of witnessing the natural world being destroyed, Attenborough has had to pivot to full eco-champion.Surviving Black Hawk DownTwo decades on from Ridley Scott’s macho war film, and more than three from the incident which inspired it, this three-part documentary returns to the moment when two US military helicopters were shot down in Somalia. Admirably fair-minded, it not only questions American military veterans – but also the surviving Somalis who witnessed their downing. It cleverly captures the chaos of war.Our review: Surviving Black Hawk Down does its utmost to render the absolute chaos of the battle while still offering context and hindsight. It’s a high-wire act, marrying calm with carnage.TrainwreckNetflix’s ever-popular documentary strand about bizarre disasters has produced some excellent watch-through-your-fingers stories. One that particularly drew attention has been the eye-catchingly titled Poop Cruise: a happy confluence of a killer name, a brilliantly scatological subject matter and some hugely entertaining contributors (“I would never expect to have a poop in a red bag”) shore up this enjoyable tale of a cruise ship left adrift in the Gulf of Mexico in 2013 following an engine fire. Helmed by Bafta-nominated director James Ross, stories unfold of bachelorette parties and people on family holidays descending into a Lord of the Flies scenario as, without any power, the toilets stop working, insanitary water pools out of the showers, and the passengers establish a shanty town on deck.Our review: Have you ever been forced to spend four days defecating into a plastic bag on a cruise ship that just caught fire and is now adrift in the Gulf of Mexico?FAQsHow much is Netflix?There are various plans available.
